questions.q: What does prototype pollution fundamentally enable an attacker to do?
choices: Add arbitrary properties to global object prototypes, which may then be inherited by user-defined objects
Directly read the private key used to sign JSON Web Tokens
Overwrite the browser's same-origin policy for a single request
Force the server to disclose its source code over HTTP
questions.explain: Prototype pollution lets an attacker add arbitrary properties to global object prototypes (most commonly Object.prototype), which are then inherited by other objects in the runtime.

questions.q: Prototype pollution vulnerabilities most typically arise when a JavaScript function does what?
choices: Recursively merges an object containing user-controllable properties into an existing object without sanitizing the keys
Encrypts user input with a weak cipher before storing it
Serializes an object to XML instead of JSON
Compares two objects using the === operator
questions.explain: The classic pattern is a recursive merge of attacker-controlled data into an existing object without first sanitizing keys like __proto__.

questions.q: Which three components are required for successful exploitation of prototype pollution?
questions.explain: Exploitation requires a source (input that poisons the prototype), a sink (a function or DOM element enabling code execution), and a gadget (a property passed to a sink without sanitization).

questions.q: What special property key is the classic vector for referencing an object's prototype during a merge operation? (one word/token)
questions.explain: Because __proto__ acts as a getter/setter for the prototype, assigning through it during a merge writes to the prototype instead of the object itself.

questions.q: Which prototype object is most commonly the target of prototype pollution?
questions.explain: Although any prototype can be polluted, pollution most commonly targets the built-in global Object.prototype because nearly all objects inherit from it.

questions.q: Which of the following are listed as common prototype pollution sources?
choices: The URL via the query or fragment string (hash)
questions.explain: The common sources are the URL (query or fragment), JSON-based input, and web messages.

questions.q: A property can serve as a gadget even if it is defined directly on the object itself.
questions.explain: If the property is defined directly on the object, the object's own version takes precedence over any malicious version added to the prototype, so it cannot be a gadget.

questions.q: For the config example where `transport_url` is used as a script src, what URL pollutes the prototype so the browser loads an attacker's script?
questions.explain: Polluting Object.prototype with a transport_url property via __proto__[transport_url] causes the config object to inherit it and set the script src to the attacker's domain.

questions.q: A JavaScript object is essentially what?
choices: A collection of key:value pairs known as properties
A reference to a database row
questions.explain: An object is a collection of key:value pairs called properties; properties holding functions are called methods.

questions.q: When you reference a property of an object, how does the JavaScript engine resolve it?
choices: It first checks the object itself, then looks up the prototype chain if not found
It only checks the object itself and returns undefined otherwise
It only checks the global Object.prototype
It checks the prototype first, then the object
questions.explain: The engine tries the object directly first; if the property is not found, it searches the object's prototype, continuing up the prototype chain.

questions.q: At the top of the prototype chain, what is the prototype of Object.prototype?
questions.explain: The chain ultimately leads back to the top-level Object.prototype, whose own prototype is null.

questions.q: `__proto__` serves as both a getter and a setter for an object's prototype.
questions.explain: __proto__ can be used both to read the prototype (and its properties) and to reassign it.

questions.q: Which method returns the prototype of a given object, e.g. Object.____(myObject) returns Object.prototype? Give the full method name.
questions.explain: Object.getPrototypeOf(myObject) returns the object's prototype, such as Object.prototype for a plain object literal.

questions.q: Why does `objectFromJson.hasOwnProperty('__proto__')` return true while the equivalent object literal returns false?
choices: JSON.parse() treats __proto__ as an ordinary string key, so it becomes an own property
hasOwnProperty is broken for all strings
Object literals always create a __proto__ own property
JSON.parse() deletes the prototype of the result
questions.explain: JSON.parse() treats any key, including __proto__, as an arbitrary string, so the parsed object gets a genuine own __proto__ property, unlike the literal where __proto__ is interpreted specially.

questions.q: To manually confirm you polluted the prototype after visiting ?__proto__[foo]=bar, what should you check in the browser console?
choices: Object.prototype.foo returns 'bar' (undefined means the attack failed)
questions.explain: Inspecting Object.prototype.foo in the console: 'bar' confirms pollution succeeded; undefined indicates it did not.

questions.q: When manually hunting gadgets, what console command adds a property to Object.prototype that logs a stack trace whenever it is read?
choices: Object.defineProperty with a get() that calls console.trace() and returns 'polluted'
questions.explain: Defining the property with a getter that calls console.trace() and returns 'polluted' reveals exactly where in the app the property is accessed.

questions.q: If __proto__ is being stripped from keys, how can you still reach Object.prototype without using the __proto__ string?
questions.explain: myObject.constructor.prototype is equivalent to myObject.__proto__, giving an alternative vector when __proto__ is blocked.

questions.q: The URL ?__pro__proto__to__.gadget=payload is designed to bypass which flawed defense?
choices: Non-recursive sanitization that strips the string __proto__ only once
questions.explain: If sanitization strips __proto__ only once, removing the inner __proto__ from __pro__proto__to__ leaves a valid __proto__ string behind.

questions.q: DOM Invader can automatically detect prototype pollution sources and scan for gadgets, sometimes even generating a DOM XSS proof-of-concept.
questions.explain: DOM Invader (in Burp's browser) automates source detection and gadget scanning, and can generate a DOM XSS PoC in some cases.

questions.q: In the fetch() gadget, which undefined property of the options object can an attacker pollute to inject a malicious response-driven value leading to DOM XSS?
questions.explain: Polluting Object.prototype with a headers property (e.g. containing a malicious x-username header) is inherited by the options object passed to fetch(), which can flow into an innerHTML sink.

questions.q: A developer uses Object.defineProperty() to define a gadget property but sets no initial value. How can an attacker still control the property's value?
choices: By polluting Object.prototype with a 'value' property that the descriptor object inherits
By polluting a 'configurable' property set to true
By calling Object.freeze on the descriptor
It cannot be bypassed once defined
questions.explain: The descriptor passed to Object.defineProperty() is itself an object; if it inherits a polluted 'value' property, that attacker-controlled value is assigned to the defined property.

questions.q: What is the final JavaScript sink in the browser-APIs fetch() example where the attacker-controlled username value causes DOM XSS?
questions.explain: The username value derived from the polluted x-username header is assigned to message.innerHTML, producing DOM XSS.

questions.q: Which factors make server-side prototype pollution harder to detect than client-side?
choices: No access to the vulnerable source code
Lack of developer tools to inspect objects at runtime
Risk of inadvertently causing a denial-of-service
Pollution persists for the lifetime of the Node process
Browsers refuse to send __proto__ in requests
questions.explain: Server-side detection is harder due to no source access, no runtime inspection, the DoS risk from polluting real properties, and pollution persisting for the whole Node process lifetime.

questions.q: Why can a `for...in` loop help detect server-side prototype pollution?
choices: It iterates over enumerable inherited properties, so a polluted property can appear reflected in a response
It only iterates own properties and therefore hides pollution
It triggers a stack overflow when the prototype is polluted
questions.explain: for...in iterates over all enumerable properties including inherited ones, so an injected prototype property can show up in a response that echoes the object's properties.

questions.q: A for...in loop iterates over the non-enumerable built-in properties set by JavaScript's native constructors.
questions.explain: Built-in properties set by native constructors are non-enumerable by default, so for...in does not include them.

questions.q: For the status code override technique, what status code does Node default to if the chosen status is not a valid number in the 400-599 range?
questions.explain: If the status is not a number or falls outside 400-599, Node sets it to 500, so you must pick a code in the 400-599 range to learn whether pollution worked.

questions.q: Which Express option, when polluted, changes the indentation of JSON responses and makes an especially safe, reversible detection technique?
questions.explain: The Express 'json spaces' option controls JSON indentation; polluting it changes indentation non-destructively and can be toggled back by resetting to the default.

questions.q: In the charset override technique, polluting the prototype with which property causes a UTF-7 string to be decoded in the response?
questions.explain: Polluting with a content-type property specifying charset=utf-7 causes body-parser to decode the body as UTF-7, revealing the decoded string in the response.

questions.q: Which techniques are used to bypass input filters that block the __proto__ key for server-side prototype pollution?
choices: Obfuscating the prohibited keyword so sanitization misses it
Accessing the prototype via the constructor property
Encrypting the request body with TLS 1.3
Sending the request over HTTP/2 only
questions.explain: Filters blocking __proto__ can be bypassed by obfuscating the keyword or by using the constructor property vector; even Node's --disable-proto flags can be bypassed via the constructor technique.

questions.q: For black-box RCE detection, why is the prototype polluted with shell and NODE_OPTIONS values pointing at Burp Collaborator?
choices: To trigger a Collaborator interaction whenever a new Node child process is created, identifying controllable requests
To immediately drop a reverse shell with no further steps
To overwrite the server's TLS certificate
questions.explain: Combining a shell property with a malicious NODE_OPTIONS (e.g. --inspect pointing at Collaborator) causes an out-of-band interaction when a child process spawns, revealing which requests create controllable Node processes.

questions.q: Which child_process.fork() option can be polluted to inject arbitrary command-line arguments such as --eval for RCE?
questions.explain: fork()'s execArgv is an array of command-line arguments; if left undefined it can be polluted, and --eval lets you run arbitrary JavaScript in the child process.

questions.q: For RCE via child_process.execSync(), which two properties are polluted together to run a malicious command?
questions.explain: execSync() does not accept execArgv, but polluting both shell (the shell to use) and input (the string piped to stdin and executed) lets you run a command of your choosing; editors like Vim or ex can serve as the stdin-reading shell.

questions.q: Which method freezes a prototype so no properties can be modified or added, cutting off pollution sources?
questions.explain: Object.freeze(Object.prototype) prevents its properties from being modified and blocks adding new ones, proactively cutting off pollution sources.

questions.q: How does Object.seal() differ from Object.freeze()?
choices: Object.seal() still allows changes to the values of existing properties
Object.seal() makes the object inherit from null
questions.explain: Object.seal() prevents adding or removing properties but still allows existing property values to change, a possible compromise when freeze is not usable.

questions.q: Which method, called as Object.____(null), creates an object that inherits no properties at all (null prototype)?
questions.explain: Object.create(null) produces an object with a null prototype, so it inherits nothing and cannot be exploited via inherited gadgets.

questions.q: Why is using a Map (instead of a plain object) a safer alternative for an options store?
choices: Its get() method only returns properties defined directly on the map, not inherited ones
Maps cannot inherit any properties whatsoever
Maps reject any key containing underscores
questions.explain: A Map can still inherit polluted properties, but its built-in get() returns only properties set directly on the map (e.g. options.get('evil') is undefined), avoiding the gadget.

questions.q: Why is key sanitization via a blocklist recommended only as a stopgap rather than a long-term defense?
choices: Robust blocklisting is hard: attackers bypass it via the constructor property or obfuscation
Blocklists are impossible to implement in JavaScript
Blocklists always break the application entirely
Blocklists only work on the server, never the client
questions.explain: Blocklists that strip __proto__ can be defeated by the constructor vector or simple obfuscation, so they are a stopgap; an allowlist of permitted keys is more effective where feasible.

questions.q: PortSwigger recommends patching prototype pollution vulnerabilities even when no exploitable gadget is currently known.
questions.explain: Future updates to your code or libraries could introduce new gadgets, so the advice is to patch the pollution regardless of whether an exploitable gadget exists today.
